title: Data snooping in backtests
objectives: Recognise data snooping, and see why factor research now asks for a $t$ statistic above 3.

screens.title: Twelve lookbacks
screens.prose: A researcher backtests momentum with 12 lookbacks on 8 years of monthly data. The market is simulated with no momentum and no drift, seed 74. The table shows each lookback's Sharpe ratio on those 8 years.

state.caption: The next 7 years are hidden for now.

screens.question: Which lookback will do best over the next 7 years?

options.text: 3 months, the in-sample winner
options.why: You assumed the in-sample rank carries forward. The market has no momentum, so 0.86 is luck.

options.text: None can be singled out: each has expected Sharpe 0
12 months, the longest and steadiest
options.why: Longer lookbacks are not better when there is no momentum to find.

options.text: 7 months, the worst, as it is due a rebound
options.why: You expected bad luck to be repaid. With no momentum, the past says nothing either way.

hints.text: What could make one lookback better than another in this market?
The market was built with no momentum at all.
With nothing to find, every lookback's future Sharpe has mean 0.

feedback.correct: In a market with no momentum, every lookback expects 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the market was built to contain.

byKey.winner: You assumed the in-sample rank carries forward. The market has no momentum, so 0.86 is luck.

explain.text: Out of sample the 3-month winner made $-0.03$, and the 1-month lookback did best, at 0.54. In-sample rank told us nothing, because there was nothing to find. The spread in the middle column was luck.

canvas.caption: The next 7 years, now shown in the last column.

screens.title: The winner's next five years
screens.prose: Each run is a search over 50 noise rules for 5 years. Top: the best in-sample Sharpe. Bottom: that winner's Sharpe on the next 5 years of fresh data. With pure noise, the future is a new draw.

params.xLabel: Best in-sample Sharpe of 50 noise rules

screens.question: Run both 1,000 times. Where does the bottom histogram centre?

options.text: Near 0
Near 0.5, half the winning Sharpe
options.why: You expected the winner to keep half its edge. With pure noise it keeps none.

options.text: Near 1.0, the same as the top
options.why: You assumed a winner stays a winner. Its 1.0 came from being picked as the best.

options.text: Below 0, as winners reverse
options.why: Noise has no reason to reverse. The fresh 5 years centre on 0.

hints.text: Run both and compare where the bars pile up.
The top piles up near 1.0. Look at the bottom.
The bottom is a fresh draw of a no-skill Sharpe: mean 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at where the bottom bars pile up.

explain.text: At the top the best of 50 averages about 1.0, from luck alone. At the bottom the same winners average 0: fresh data owe nothing to an old maximum. The gap between the two is the selection bias that snooping hides.

screens.title: In sample, out of sample
screens.prose: Here is the 3-month winner, £100 invested. The rule was chosen on the first 8 years: that period is **in sample**. The last 7 years are **out of sample**: data the choice never saw.
screens.question: Which part of the curve is evidence about whether the rule has an edge?

options.text: The out-of-sample part, after month 96
The in-sample part, the shaded years
options.why: That part chose the rule. It was picked because it looked good there, so it was bound to look good.

options.text: Both parts equally
options.why: The in-sample part is the reason the rule was chosen. It cannot also be the test.

options.text: Neither part
options.why: The out-of-sample years played no part in the choice, so they are a fair test, if a short one.

hints.text: Which years did the researcher look at when choosing the lookback?
The shaded years did the choosing.
Only data not used to choose can test the choice.

feedback.correct: Only the out-of-sample years test the rule.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which years were used to pick the rule.

byKey.ins: That part chose the rule. It was picked because it looked good there, so it was bound to look good.

explain.text: Choosing the rule on the first 8 years used them up as evidence. Only the last 7 years test it, and there it went nowhere: Sharpe $-0.03$. Fitting a rule to the data it is then judged on is **overfitting**, and the search that does it is **data snooping**.

screens.title: Hundreds of factors
screens.prose: By 2012, journals had published over 300 return factors. Suppose all 300 were noise. Each $t$ statistic is then close to standard normal, and $P(|Z| > 2) = 0.0455$.
screens.question: How many of 300 noise factors would show $|t| > 2$? Give 2 decimal places.

widget.label: Expected false factors at the t > 2 bar

hints.text: Each noise factor passes with chance 0.0455.
Read the $|t| > 2$ line where it crosses 300 factors.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the number of factors by the chance each passes.

byKey.five: You used 0.05. The two-sided chance of $|t| > 2$ is 0.0455, a little less.
byKey.one: That is one factor's chance. There were 300.

explain.text: $300 \times 0.0455 = 13.65$: about 14 published factors from noise alone at the usual bar. Far more than 300 were tried and never published. That is why the bar had to move.

screens.title: The $t > 3$ rule
screens.prose: Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016) argued that a new factor should clear $t > 3$, not 2. For a noise factor, $P(|Z| > 3) = 0.0027$.
screens.question: How many of 300 noise factors would clear $|t| > 3$? Give 2 decimal places.

widget.label: Expected false factors at the t > 3 bar

hints.text: Same sum, new chance.
Read the $|t| > 3$ line where it crosses 300 factors.

byKey.two: That is the count at the old bar of 2. Use $P(|Z| > 3) = 0.0027$.

explain.text: $300 \times 0.0027 = 0.81$: under one false factor expected, down from 13.65. The bar of 3 is a multiple-testing correction for a field that has tried hundreds of ideas. Bonferroni for 300 tests would ask even more, $|t| > 3.76$.

screens.title: Peeking at the test set
screens.prose: A researcher holds out 2020 to 2024 as a test set. Her first rule fails there. She tweaks it and re-tests on the same years, 20 times, then keeps the best: attempt 16, with a test Sharpe of 1.11.

state.caption: Twenty rules with no edge, seed 50

screens.question: What is her test Sharpe of 1.11 now worth as evidence?

options.text: Strong: it was measured on held-out data
options.why: You trusted the label test set. After 20 looks it has become training data: 1.11 is the best of 20 tries on it.

options.text: Little: it is the best of 20 tries on the same data, so the test set is spent
Strong, once halved for safety
options.why: No fixed haircut repairs this. She ran 20 tests, and the hold-out is no longer held out.

options.text: Nothing, since a test set is never valid
options.why: A test set used once is valid. It is the 20 looks that spent it.

hints.text: How many times did the test set judge a rule?
Each bar is one look at the same five years.
The best of 20 noise tries on 5 years averages about $1.87 / \sqrt 5 = 0.84$.

feedback.correct: Twenty looks turned the test set into a search.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how many rules the test set has judged.

byKey.held-out: You trusted the label test set. After 20 looks it has become training data: 1.11 is the best of 20 tries on it.

explain.text: Each re-test was a new test on the same 5 years. The best of 20 noise tries averages a Sharpe of $1.87 / \sqrt 5 = 0.84$, so 1.11 is unremarkable. A test set tells the truth only the first time you look.

screens.title: Snooping's cousins
screens.prose: Other mistakes also feed a backtest information it would not have had. **Survivorship bias** you met in *Survivorship bias*. **Look-ahead bias** uses data before it was available.
screens.question: Match each backtest to its flaw.

tokens.text: Testing 50 lookbacks and reporting the best one
Backtesting today's FTSE 100 members over 20 years
Buying at the close on a signal computed from that same close

hints.text: Ask what each backtest knew that a trader at the time could not.
Today's index members are the firms that survived.
The best of 50 is snooping; today's members is survivorship; trading on a close you could not yet see is look-ahead.

feedback.correct: Selection, survivors and the future: three ways to know too much.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each backtest knew that a trader at the time could not.

explain.text: Reporting the best of 50 hides 49 tests: snooping. Today's members leave out the firms that failed: survivorship. A signal from a close you cannot yet see uses the future: look-ahead.

screens.title: Theory first
screens.prose: Edge case. In 2014 an economist publishes a model that predicts a carry effect, with the exact rule and test written down. The rule is then run once on 2015 to 2024 data: $t = 2.3$.

params.xLabel: $t$ statistic if there is no effect

screens.question: How many tests should the correction count?

options.text: One: the rule and the test were fixed before the data
Every carry paper ever written
options.why: Other people's tests on other data do not touch this one. This rule was fixed before any looking.

options.text: Assume 100, to be safe
options.why: Counting tests that never happened throws away real evidence.

options.text: None, since a theory needs no test
options.why: The theory still has to meet the data, in one test at the usual bar.

hints.text: How many rules were tried on 2015 to 2024 data?
The shaded tail is the chance a single no-effect test gives $t \ge 2.3$.
Fixed in advance and run once: $N = 1$.

feedback.correct: One test, so $t = 2.3$ meets the plain bar.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the rules that were run on the new data.

explain.text: The rule was fixed before the data existed, and run once: $N = 1$. So $t = 2.3$ meets the plain bar, with one-sided $p = 0.011$. No snooping happened, so no penalty is due.

screens.title: An honest protocol
screens.prose: An honest backtest makes the count of tests known and the final test clean. Each step closes one door to snooping.
screens.question: Put the protocol in order.

lines.text: Write down the hypothesis, the rule and the hold-out period, before seeing the data
Tune any parameters on the training data only
Run the final rule on the hold-out, once
Report the result with the count of everything tried

hints.text: What has to happen before anyone looks at the data?
The hold-out is used after all tuning is finished.
Plan, tune on training data, one run on the hold-out, then report.

feedback.correct: Plan, tune, test once, report everything.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fix the plan first and touch the hold-out last.

byKey.once: The hold-out run must come after tuning, or tuning leaks into it.
byKey.plan: The plan comes first, before any data are seen.

explain.text: The plan fixes $N$ before the data can suggest anything. Tuning stays off the hold-out, and one run keeps it honest. Reporting the count lets any reader apply the right correction.

screens.title: The best window
screens.prose: A momentum paper tries 50 lookback windows and reports the best: a Sharpe of 0.9 over 10 years, so $t = 0.9\sqrt{10} = 2.85$. The one-sided Bonferroni bar for 50 tries is $z_{0.999} = 3.09$.

params.yLabel: Sharpe the best must clear, 10 years

screens.question: Does the reported window pass?

options.text: Yes: 2.85 is far above 1.645
options.why: You used the bar for one test. The paper tried 50 windows.

options.text: No: 2.85 is below the bar of 3.09
Yes: 2.85 is close enough to 3
options.why: Close is not past. The bar exists because the best of 50 often gets near it by luck.

options.text: No: a Sharpe of 0.9 can never be significant
options.why: It can, with a long enough record: 0.9 over 12 years gives $t = 3.12$.

hints.text: Which bar applies to the best of 50?
The marked point is the bar for 50 windows over 10 years; the paper's 0.9 is the dashed line.

feedback.correct: 2.85 is short of 3.09: the window does not pass.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $t = 2.85$ with the bar for the best of 50.

byKey.one: You used the bar for one test. The paper tried 50 windows.

explain.text: The best of 50 must clear $t = 3.09$, a Sharpe of $3.09/\sqrt{10} = 0.98$ over 10 years. At 0.9 the paper falls short. With 12 years the same Sharpe would give $t = 3.12$ and pass.

screens.title: A model with a validation set
screens.prose: A preview of Stage 2. A machine-learning model is tuned over 200 hyperparameter settings, each scored on a validation set. The best scores a Sharpe of 1.3 there.
screens.question: What is the honest next step?

options.text: Score the chosen model once on the untouched test years
Report 1.3 as the expected live Sharpe
options.why: 1.3 is the best of 200 on the validation data, so it is biased upward like any best-of-many.

options.text: Refit on validation and test together, then score on both
options.why: Scoring on data used for fitting is in-sample. Nothing would be left to test with.

options.text: Try 200 more settings to be sure
options.why: More tries only raise the maximum that luck can reach on the validation set.

hints.text: Which slice has played no part in the choice?
The validation slice chose the model, so it is spent.
Use the test years, once.

feedback.correct: One clean run on the test years.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the data that played no part in fitting or choosing.

explain.text: The validation set picked the best of 200, so 1.3 carries the same selection bias as a backtest search. The test years are the hold-out: score once, and report that number with the count of 200. That is the honest protocol in machine-learning dress.

ideas: A rule chosen on some data looks good there by construction. Only data the choice never saw can test it.
With hundreds of factors tried, $|t| > 2$ lets about 14 noise factors through per 300. That is why factor research asks for $t > 3$.
Specify first, tune on training data, test once on a hold-out, and report everything tried. A rule fixed before the data needs no penalty.
summary.trap: Re-testing on the test set until it looks good turns the test set into training data.

quiz.prose: You are handed a backtest with a strong Sharpe ratio.
quiz.question: Select all that apply: which questions belong on a checklist for reading any backtest?

options.text: How many variants were tried before this one?
Was data held out, and looked at only once?
Does the universe include firms that later failed?
Was every signal built only from data available at the time?
Is the in-sample Sharpe above 2?
options.why: A high in-sample number is what snooping produces. It is not a check.

options.text: Does the in-sample equity curve look smooth?
options.why: A smooth curve in sample is easy to fit. It says nothing about the future.

feedback.correct: Count the tries, check the hold-out, the survivors and the timing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the questions that expose snooping and its cousins.

explain.text: The first four expose snooping, a spent hold-out, survivorship and look-ahead. The last two describe the result, not how it was made. A good-looking in-sample curve is exactly what a search produces.

quiz.prose: A database holds 500 factor definitions, all of them noise. Use $P(|Z| > 3) = 0.0027$.
quiz.question: How many are expected to clear $|t| > 3$? Give 2 decimal places.

byKey.two: That is the count at $|t| > 2$. Use 0.0027.

explain.text: $500 \times 0.0027 = 1.35$. Even the stricter bar lets about one noise factor through in 500. The more factors a field tries, the higher the bar must go.

quiz.prose: The 3-month lookback from the lesson had Sharpe 0.86 over 8 years, so $t = 0.86\sqrt 8 = 2.43$. It was the best of 12. The one-sided Bonferroni bar for 12 is $z_{1 - 0.05/12} = 2.64$.
quiz.question: Does it pass the corrected bar?

options.text: No: 2.43 is below 2.64
Yes: 2.43 is above 1.645
options.why: You used the one-test bar. It was the best of 12.

options.text: Yes: 2.43 is above 2
options.why: You used the rough two-sided bar for one test. It was chosen from 12.

feedback.correct: 2.43 falls short of 2.64, and the market had no momentum.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare 2.43 with the bar for the best of 12.

explain.text: Against one test, 2.43 would look strong, with one-sided $p = 0.008$. As the best of 12, it must clear 2.64, and it does not. The correction got it right: the simulated market had no momentum.

quiz.prose: Four strategies each show $t = 2.4$ on 10 years of data.
quiz.question: Which one needs no snooping penalty?

options.text: A rule set out in a 2014 paper, run once on 2015 to 2024
A rule whose threshold was tuned on 2015 to 2024
options.why: Tuning on the same years makes them in-sample. The tuning was a search.

options.text: The best of 8 rules run on 2015 to 2024
options.why: That is a family of 8. The best must clear a higher bar.

options.text: A rule tested on today's index members over 2015 to 2024
options.why: No snooping, perhaps, but survivorship bias inflates the result.

feedback.correct: Fixed in advance and run once: $N = 1$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the rule that was fixed before the data were seen.

explain.text: Only the 2014 rule was fixed before the data and run once, so $N = 1$. The tuned rule and the best of 8 are searches. The survivor test has its own bias.
